--- title: "Data" subtitle: "Where the shade and heat maps come from, and who we follow home." jupyter: python3 --- ## Sources All inputs are public. | Layer | Source | Used for | | --- | --- | --- | | Airborne LiDAR, March 2022 | City of Philadelphia (NOAA Digital Coast, PASDA) | ground, building and tree heights at 1 m | | Building footprints | City of Philadelphia | building outlines | | Land cover 2018 | PASDA | tree canopy | | Canopy height (CHMv2) | Meta / WRI, CC BY 4.0 | trees just outside the city | | Pedestrian network | DVRPC | sidewalks and crosswalks | | OpenStreetMap | OSM contributors, ODbL | bridges, covered walkways, campus footways | | Transit | SEPTA, fall 2026 timetable | stations and frequent bus stops | | Properties | City of Philadelphia (OPA) | homes, where walks end | | Hourly weather | ERA5 (ECMWF), via Open-Meteo | weather for the heat model | | Heat model | SOLWEIG 2022a (solweig-gpu 2.0.0) | felt temperature (UTCI) at 1 m | | Surface temperature, air temperature | USGS Landsat 8; NOAA ACIS | heat figures on the Story page | ## The shade map ::: {.stat-row}

::: Heights come from the 2022 LiDAR survey. Building heights match the city's records to 0.5 m (median, 541,222 buildings); bridges and elevated rail cast shadows too. Trees cover 17% of the city (median height 15 m). Covered walkways (4.2 km) are always in shade. ::: {#0879cbdc .cell .figure-light execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ![University City in the height model: buildings (blue and pink), bridges and other structures (orange) and trees (green).](data_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.jpeg){} ::: ::: ## The heat model Shade says where the sun is blocked, not how hot a sidewalk feels. For that, the same heights go into SOLWEIG, which computes the radiation a standing person receives from sun, sky, walls and ground and, with the weather, the **UTCI**: how hot it feels, in °C. Above 38 °C is *very strong* heat stress, above 46 °C *extreme*. The model needs real weather, so the study uses two hot, sunny days of 2025: **June 24**, during a heat wave, and **July 29**. Shadows are computed for the same moments. | Day | Air temperature, 15:00 | Humidity, 15:00 | Wind, 15:00 | Peak solar radiation | Daily maximum | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | June 24, 2025 | 38.5 °C | 32% | 2.8 m/s | 936 W/m² | 38.8 °C | | July 29, 2025 | 36.1 °C | 43% | 1.8 m/s | 914 W/m² | 36.1 °C | One ERA5 cell covers the whole city, so air temperature and wind are the same everywhere; the heat map varies with sun, shade, walls and ground. The model ran in 400 one-kilometre tiles per day on a GPU and gives a UTCI value at all 3.6 million sidewalk points, every hour. ## Whose walks Each walk starts at a rapid-transit station (Regional Rail, L, B, T tunnel) or at a bus stop with at least 6 buses an hour (15:00–19:00), and ends at a home within 1.2 km on foot: 431,114 walks. The other 91,659 homes (17.5%), mostly in the Northeast and Roxborough, have no frequent stop that close. ::: {#bb39a9d6 .cell .figure-light execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ![Homes without a frequent stop within 1.2 km (red).](data_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.jpeg){width=640} ::: ::: ## University City In University City, entrances and indoor passages of 41 buildings were mapped (4.4 km; 10 buildings open without a Penn ID), and campus footpaths from OpenStreetMap were added. ## Known gaps - Campus and park paths are missing outside University City, so cooler options there are understated. - Two clear, hot days; trees from leaf-off LiDAR and 2018 land cover, buildings from 2022. - One weather cell for the city: no neighbourhood differences in air temperature or wind. Trees let a fixed 3% of the sun through. - Missing footprints, new buildings and temporary objects affect shade locally. - The timetable is one weekday in fall 2026.
